meta.title: The Complete Writer's Compendium — Attributions
meta.description: All sources, quotes, principles, and concept attributions used in the compendium, grouped by chapter and type.

attributions.text: 10% is talent, 90% is craft.
attributions.paraphrase: What matters most is not talent but self-discipline, persistence, and absolute stamina.
attributions.source_work: How to Write a Damn Good Novel
attributions.source_work_original_title: How to Write a Damn Good Novel
attributions.source_work_german_title: Wie man einen verdammt guten Roman schreibt
attributions.notes: Widely paraphrased; core thesis of Frey's guide.

attributions.text: Master the rules first, then transcend them.
attributions.paraphrase: Picasso had a 10-year career of conventional work before going wild. Know the rules before breaking them intentionally.
attributions.source_work: Helping Writers Become Authors (K.M. Weiland blog)
attributions.notes: Principle widely cited in craft discussions; Picasso analogy from K.M. Weiland.

attributions.text: Put the work away for a while before editing. When you return with fresh eyes, you'll see clearly what needs to change.
attributions.source_work: 10 Dos & Don'ts For the Aspiring Novelist
attributions.notes: Advice on temporal distance before self-editing.

attributions.text: Successful storytelling is largely about managing (and creating) reader expectations.
attributions.source_work: The Rules of Fiction: What They Are and What They're Not

attributions.text: Every character should want something, even if it is only a glass of water.
attributions.source_work: Worldbuilding 101: Writing Consistent Characters and Building Realistic Worlds
attributions.publisher: We Need Diverse Books (cited via Sarah Guan, Erewhon Books)
attributions.notes: One of Vonnegut's most-cited pieces of writing advice. Originally from his 8 rules of short story writing.

attributions.text: Three Dimensions of Character: External Want, Internal Need, Fatal Flaw / Wound
attributions.attributed_to: Multiple sources; widely established in craft literature
attributions.source_work: Various — including Sol Stein (On Writing), James N. Frey, K.M. Weiland (Helping Writers Become Authors)
attributions.notes: The want/need/wound framework is a foundational concept in modern craft pedagogy, not attributable to a single author.

attributions.text: The 'As You Know, Bob' Problem — expository dialogue where characters explain things they both already know, solely for the reader's benefit.
attributions.attributed_to: Unknown origin; widely used in craft communities
attributions.source_work: Best Practices: Deep Lore and World Building, Choice of Games Forum
attributions.notes: A named craft concept with no single originator. Named after the phrase pattern 'As you know, Bob...' Sometimes called the 'maid and butler' dialogue problem.

attributions.text: Tolkien invented languages for decades before publishing The Hobbit. He started world-building from the bottom up — languages first.
attributions.source_work: How To Write Lore (And Build A Rich, Expansive World)
attributions.notes: Referenced across multiple writing craft articles as a canonical example of deep world-building.

attributions.text: The Iceberg Principle of World-Building: for every detail on the page, ten must exist in the author's mind.
attributions.attributed_to: Ernest Hemingway (original iceberg theory of omission); applied to world-building by multiple craft writers
attributions.source_work: Worldbuilding Tips for Fiction Writers: A Complete Guide (Sudowrite)
attributions.notes: Hemingway's iceberg theory of omission applied to world-building. The specific world-building application is widespread in craft communities.

attributions.text: Build outward from your protagonist's experience. What do they see, touch, and bump against? Build from there.
attributions.source_work: Worldbuilding Tips for Fiction Writers: A Complete Guide
attributions.notes: Reaction against Tolkienesque pre-publication world-building; attributed to contemporary craft pedagogy.

attributions.text: Six World-Building Categories: Settings, Items, Lore, Factions, Rules, Custom
attributions.source_work: Worldbuilding Tips for Fiction Writers: A Complete Guide
attributions.notes: Adapted into a general framework for the compendium.

attributions.text: Lore: a body of traditions and knowledge on a subject or held by a particular group, typically passed from person to person by word of mouth.
attributions.attributed_to: Dictionary definition, applied to fiction by J.D. Edwin
attributions.source_work: How to Write Lore That Will Deepen Your Fantasy World
attributions.notes: J.D. Edwin defines and contextualizes lore as 'a story your characters would tell.'

attributions.text: Lore is a story your characters would tell — it invites readers to ask questions rather than passively receiving information.
attributions.source_work: How to Write Lore That Will Deepen Your Fantasy World

attributions.text: Das Unbekannte um die Ränder der Szene — wie Kafkas Schloss oder der Prozess — existiert spürbar, ohne je vollständig erklärt zu werden.
attributions.source_work: Das Schloss (1926); Der Proceß (1925)
attributions.notes: Used as a German literary example of the iceberg principle — the bureaucratic world is sensed but never fully explained.

attributions.text: Character-based world-building: use each scene to explore the world through a character's point of view.
attributions.source_work: How Characters Shape Worldbuilding — The Weird Circular

attributions.text: Everything is worldbuilding. Worldbuilding has this negative connotation as sort of this homework that you have to do beforehand… Everything in a story is worldbuilding in the same way that everything about us is worldbuilding.
attributions.attributed_to: Unnamed speaker (quoted in H.L. Walrath newsletter)
attributions.source_work: How Characters Shape Worldbuilding — The Weird Circular
attributions.notes: Speaker identity not confirmed in source.

attributions.text: The Three-Act Structure: Act I (25%), Act II-A (25%), Act II-B (25%), Act III (25%)
attributions.attributed_to: Aristotle (original); modern codification via Syd Field, Robert McKee, and others
attributions.source_work: Story: Substance, Structure, Style and the Principles of Screenwriting — Robert McKee (1997); widely cited in prose craft
attributions.notes: The 25/25/25/25 percentage split is a common approximation used in modern craft guides. Not a single-author formulation.

attributions.text: Show, Don't Tell: convey information through action, dialogue, and sensory details rather than direct exposition.
attributions.attributed_to: Anton Chekhov (widely attributed); popularized in 20th-century creative writing pedagogy
attributions.source_work: Common Writing Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them (Fiveable); multiple sources
attributions.notes: One of the most widely cited craft principles. The Chekhov attribution is disputed; the principle was formalized in the 20th century MFA tradition.

attributions.text: Filter words: words like 'felt,' 'saw,' 'noticed,' 'heard,' 'thought' that place a narrator between reader and experience. Removing them creates immediacy.
attributions.attributed_to: Susan Leigh Needham; Deep POV craft tradition
attributions.source_work: Line Level Edit - Checklist for Writers
attributions.notes: Filter words are also covered in Jill Elizabeth Nelson's 'Rivet Your Readers With Deep Point Of View.'

attributions.text: Deep Point of View (Deep POV): a technique that eliminates filtering and places the reader directly inside the character's experience.
attributions.source_work: Rivet Your Readers With Deep Point Of View
attributions.notes: Cited as best resource for Deep POV by Susan Leigh Needham.

attributions.text: Purple prose: a type of writing in which the extravagant style and use of language gets in the way of the narrative. The work of a writer lost in the form of language, leading them to neglect the function of language.
attributions.source_work: Purple Prose: What It Is, Examples & How to Avoid It

attributions.text: Purple: 'The tall, brooding, mysterious stranger walked solemnly and silently across the desolate, fog-laced, moonlit street.' Better: 'The stranger drifted down the fog-laced street, quiet and unreadable.'
attributions.source_work: Writing 101: Avoiding Purple Prose

attributions.text: When you catch an adjective, kill it. Not always, not often, but whenever you can.
attributions.source_work: Letter to D.W. Bowser, March 20, 1880 (widely cited)
attributions.notes: One of the most famous pieces of prose style advice. Exact original source is a letter.

attributions.text: Faulkner vs Hemingway on prose density: Faulkner ranked Hemingway low for never using a word that might cause the reader to check with a dictionary. Hemingway later responded in kind.
attributions.source_work: 1947 University of Mississippi Q&A (published in The Western Review); cited in Purple Prose article by Alan Watt
attributions.notes: Illustrates that the debate between ornate and spare prose has a long literary history.

attributions.text: Passive voice is not a grammatical error — it is a stylistic issue pertaining to clarity. Use it intentionally, not by default.
attributions.source_work: Passive Voice — The Writing Center
attributions.notes: Corrects the common misconception that passive voice is always wrong.

attributions.text: Head-hopping: when the Point of View (POV) changes mid-scene or mid-paragraph, confusing the reader by jumping between characters' internal perspectives without a structural break.
attributions.source_work: Common Manuscript Issues - Advice from An Editorial Consultant
attributions.notes: Distinguished from legitimate multi-POV structure, which uses scene or chapter breaks.

attributions.text: Three Levels of Self-Editing: Story Level, Scene Level, Line Level — must be addressed in this order.
attributions.source_work: Line Level Edit - Checklist for Writers (Revision Levels Series)
attributions.notes: The macro-to-micro editing order is standard in developmental editing; Needham's framing is the primary source used.

attributions.text: Rule #1: Consider every editorial suggestion seriously — ask why the editor made it. Rule #2: You don't have to take the editor's specific fix — but the problem they identified is almost certainly real. It's your story.
attributions.source_work: Two Simple Rules of Editing
attributions.notes: Emily's Rule #1 and Rule #2. Practical framework for author-editor collaboration.

attributions.text: Even editors have editors. You can't see your own work unbiased.
attributions.source_work: Two Simple Rules of Editing

attributions.text: Sol Stein: Über das Schreiben
attributions.source_work: Über das Schreiben (German translation of 'Stein on Writing')
attributions.notes: Considered the comprehensive standard reference in German craft circles.

attributions.text: James N. Frey: Wie man einen verdammt guten Roman schreibt
attributions.source_work: Wie man einen verdammt guten Roman schreibt (German translation)
attributions.source_work_original_title: How to Write a Damn Good Novel
attributions.notes: One of the two most-recommended German craft guides. Praised for its direct, practical tone.

attributions.text: Dorothea Brande: Schriftsteller werden
attributions.source_work: Schriftsteller werden (German translation of 'Becoming a Writer')
attributions.notes: Despite being from 1934, praised as timeless on creative process, writer identity, and overcoming blocks.

attributions.text: Robert McKee: Story — Die Prinzipien des Drehbuchschreibens
attributions.source_work: Story (German edition)
attributions.source_work_original_title: Story: Substance, Structure, Style and the Principles of Screenwriting
attributions.notes: Recommended for prose writers despite being a screenwriting guide. German community finds screenwriting guides clearer and more actionable.

attributions.text: Isa Schikorsky: Aus dem Lektorat — 50 Tipps zum Schreiben und Veröffentlichen
attributions.source_work: Aus dem Lektorat: 50 Tipps zum Schreiben und Veröffentlichen
attributions.notes: Written by a working editor and author; highly practical, covering prose-writing tips and the German publishing market.

attributions.text: Fritz Gesing: Kreativ Schreiben — Handwerk und Techniken des Erzählens
attributions.source_work: Kreativ Schreiben. Handwerk und Techniken des Erzählens
attributions.notes: Theoretical but grounded in analysis of known novels. Suited for understanding narrative structure.

attributions.text: Stephen King: On Writing — A Memoir of the Craft
attributions.source_work: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft
attributions.notes: Memoir + craft guide. Widely cited for voice, habit, and storytelling instinct.

attributions.text: William Strunk Jr. & E.B. White: The Elements of Style
attributions.attributed_to: William Strunk Jr. and E.B. White
attributions.source_work: The Elements of Style
attributions.notes: Cited as foundational reference for sentence-level craft and clarity. 4th edition (2000) is current.

attributions.text: Angela Ackerman & Becca Puglisi: The Emotion Thesaurus — A Writer's Guide to Character Expression
attributions.source_work: The Emotion Thesaurus: A Writer's Guide to Character Expression
attributions.notes: Reference tool for physical/behavioral expressions of emotion. Used for Show-Don't-Tell craft. Available in 5 languages; sourced by US universities.

attributions.text: Dwight Swain: Techniques of the Selling Writer
attributions.source_work: Techniques of the Selling Writer
attributions.notes: Advanced craft guide. Covers scene/sequel structure, motivation-reaction units, plot architecture. Highly recommended by German advanced writers despite English-only availability.

attributions.text: Jeff VanderMeer: Wonderbook — The Illustrated Guide to Creating Imaginative Fiction
attributions.source_work: Wonderbook: The Illustrated Guide to Creating Imaginative Fiction (Revised & Expanded)
attributions.notes: Speculative fiction world-building; visual and highly creative. Contributors include George R.R. Martin and Ursula K. Le Guin.

attributions.text: James Wood: How Fiction Works
attributions.source_work: How Fiction Works
attributions.notes: Advanced literary analysis of technique. Covers deep POV, free indirect style, prose voice. For literary fiction writers.

attributions.text: Anne Lamott: Bird by Bird — Some Instructions on Writing and Life
attributions.source_work: Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life
attributions.notes: Mindset and process. Famous for the 'shitty first drafts' chapter — permission to write badly before writing well.

attributions.text: Jessica Brody: Save the Cat! Writes a Novel
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat! Writes a Novel: The Last Book on Novel Writing You'll Ever Need
attributions.notes: Applies Blake Snyder's Save the Cat screenwriting beat sheet to novel structure. Very popular with beginner-intermediate writers.

attributions.text: Showing allows readers to experience the story alongside the characters. Telling simply states information without engaging the reader.
attributions.source_work: Common Writing Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

attributions.text: Start strong on page one. Ensure first pages establish a scene, create conflict, or generate a mystery — possibly all three. This is why editors and agents often dislike prologues.
attributions.source_work: Self-Editing: Follow These 10 Golden Rules
attributions.notes: A prologue is typically all backstory and rarely delivers scene, conflict, or mystery.

attributions.text: Don't fall in love with your words. Be able to read your work with a critical eye and cut excess or clunky writing.
attributions.source_work: 10 Dos & Don'ts For the Aspiring Novelist

attributions.text: World-building checklist: geography, history, inhabitants, culture/customs, language, politics/power, rules (magic/tech), economy.
attributions.source_work: How to Write a Believable World: A Guide to Worldbuilding
attributions.notes: Synthesized from multiple world-building guides.

attributions.text: Always move the plot forward. Flashbacks or trips into the past are fine if revisiting a character's history in some way progresses your plot.
attributions.attributed_to: Kate Foster (freelance editor, Ink Pantry Publishing)
attributions.source_work: 7 Writing Rules For Fiction
attributions.notes: Rule #2 of Foster's fiction rules, based on recurring problems seen while editing manuscripts.

attributions.text: Mastering Deep POV writing will virtually eliminate Show-Don't-Tell issues in manuscripts.
attributions.source_work: Line Level Edit - Checklist for Writers
attributions.notes: Recommends 'Rivet Your Readers With Deep Point Of View' by Jill Elizabeth Nelson as the primary Deep POV resource.

attributions.text: Das deutsche Literaturverständnis ist bis ins 21. Jahrhundert von der Genieästhetik geprägt — der Idee, dass echte Kunst nicht an Regeln gebunden sein darf.
attributions.attributed_to: Halupczok (cited in academic paper on Creative Writing in Germany)
attributions.source_work: Über die Bedeutung von Creative Writing im Land der Dichter und Denker
attributions.notes: Explains why the German craft-guide tradition developed later than the Anglo-American one and why 'Schreiben' was long considered unteachable in Germany.
